Price and disruption context 2022 · 2024 · 2025/26
EVENT ANNOTATIONSDescriptive context; no event effect estimated
2022 / CROP + INSPECTION

Prices rose before the pause

January shipping-point Hass cartons: $48.94 vs $23.05 a year earlier. Mexico's crop was forecast 8% lower; the inspection pause came February 12–18. [11]

2024 / SIZE MIX

More units, higher retail ASP

Retail units rose 4% and annual ASP rose 12% to $1.19 per fruit. Large fruit was scarcer; a June inspection pause also occurred. Neither effect is isolated. [12–14]

2025/26 / RECOVERY

Large fruit returned

Large-size share rose from 40% to 50% of Mexico's season-to-date U.S. shipments. Mid-March 2026 FOB was near $1/lb, about one-third of a year earlier. [8]

Extra non-Mexico flow →
Model formula and limits

Lost Mexico flow = observed monthly Mexico tonnes ÷ days in month × 7 × weeks × loss share; subtract assumed extra non-Mexico flow and one-time buffer, floored at zero. An eight-week run repeats the selected month's rate. This is a stress test, not a calendar or price forecast. [2]

04 / SOURCING RESPONSE

What I would do as the buyer.

  1. 01 / PROTECT

    Protect Mexico. Confirm crossings, packhouses, and usable inventory. Observed concentration · retailer plan unverified

  2. 02 / QUALIFY

    Buy seasonal options. Trial Peru and Colombia by week, size, grade, and pack. Observed timing · capacity unverified

  3. 03 / TRIGGER

    Adjust promotions before stockouts. Tie decisions to confirmed receipts and DC inventory. Analyst recommendation · retailer data needed

Execution needs retailer POS, contracts, inventory, shrink, and SKU costs. A food-swap signal needs local prices and availability; it isn't calculated here.

BEFORE COUNTING REPLACEMENT SUPPLY

What I would ask a supplier tomorrow.

Historic shipments prove a lane existed. These answers determine whether it can cover a specific retail order.

  1. Which weeks and firm tonnes can you commit beyond existing customer contracts?
  2. Which Hass sizes, grades, ripeness specs, and bag or bulk packs can you supply?
  3. What are packhouse throughput, cold-chain capacity, lead time, and route variance?
  4. What U.S. phytosanitary requirements apply to this fruit and origin?
  5. What is the delivered cost by SKU, including shrink and claims?
  6. What happens to the commitment if inspection or freight is interrupted?

STATUS · UNVERIFIED COMMERCIAL INPUTS. None is inferred from national production or bilateral exports.

SUPPLIER OPTIONS / OBSERVED FLOWS

Which alternatives can help—and when?

These are sourcing candidates, not a ranked capacity forecast. U.S. lane sizes come from 2025 imports; non-U.S. export volumes and destinations use 2024 reporter data. [2, 3]

DOMESTIC BUFFER

California

Domestic shipments rise in spring and peak in summer, according to USDA ERS. They can complement summer imports, but are not part of this import-reallocation model. [8]

DEVELOPMENT PATH

Guatemala

APHIS updated the systems-approach requirements for Hass avocados in 2025, including a joint operational workplan and pest controls. ERS records no U.S. import flow in this snapshot for 2024–25; this is a qualification prospect, not modeled replacement volume. [9]

Peak three-month windows are descriptive shares of each origin’s 2025 U.S. shipments. A destination such as the Netherlands is the reported trade partner, not necessarily the final consumer or physical route. The Dominican Republic’s U.S. supply is predominantly non-Hass, so product fit requires separate assessment. [8]

AT THE RETAIL EDGE / PRICE EVIDENCE

What shoppers see—and what they pay.

Retail prices sit downstream of import costs. These two USDA measures capture different parts of that market and use different units.

WEEKLY ADVERTISED PRICE · CONVENTIONAL HASS · EACH—

National grocery-store promotions · report loading

Advertised prices are promotional offers, not transaction-weighted checkout averages. [6]

SCANNER-DATA RETAIL ESTIMATE · 2023 · PER POUND—

USDA ERS estimate of the average price paid for fresh avocados in 2023, based on Circana retail scanner data. [7]

Two lenses, two units.

One is a weekly advertised price per fruit; the other is an annual transaction-based estimate per pound. The Atlas does not subtract them or feed either into its import-cost scenario.

RETAIL FORMAT / THE HIDDEN CAPACITY TEST

The fruit must fit the shelf.

A sourcing plan must specify pack format and fruit size as well as origin. The Hass Avocado Board's Circana analysis shows why this matters. [10]

THE 2022 FORMAT SIGNAL+9.4 points

Bagged fruit's share rose from 19.0% in 2019 to 28.4% in 2022. Small 4- and 5-count bags generated 54% of bagged avocado dollar sales in 2022. [10]

BUYER'S TEST

Ask prospective suppliers for packhouse throughput by bag count and fruit size, packaging materials, ripening specifications, and delivered cost by SKU. Tonnes alone cannot confirm a retail-ready replacement.

NEXT CONSTRAINT

The next bottleneck is not where avocados grow. It is how much existing export supply can be diverted, in season, through U.S.-accessible channels.

OBSERVED 2024 ENTRY PATTERN86% through the Laredo customs district · 6% Philadelphia · 5% Miami [4]District shares describe recorded entry, not available spare capacity or exact shipment routes.

RISK REGISTER / EVIDENCE TO ACTION

Where the chain could fail.

Risk signals are observed. The responses are analyst recommendations to validate with suppliers, buyers, and import authorities.

01 / ORIGIN & ENTRY

One supplier, one major entry corridor

Mexico supplied 83.4% of 2025 import volume. In 2024, 86% of fresh avocado imports entered through the Laredo customs district. These are separate measures, both pointing to concentrated exposure. [2, 4]

Decision

Map alternate entry arrangements and test continuity plans with existing Mexican partners before a disruption.

02 / CALENDAR FIT

Alternatives peak after winter exposure

Mexico supplied 95.2% of U.S. imports in January–April 2024. Peru’s 2025 U.S. shipments peaked in June–August. A large annual export pool cannot automatically cover a winter shortfall. [2, 8]

Decision

Contract and test supply by month, size, and grade; measure the gap for the exact weeks that matter.

03 / COMPETING BUYERS

Export volume is already allocated

Peru and Colombia sell substantial volume outside the U.S.; USDA ERS reports that more than half of their fresh exports go to the EU. The 2024 FAOSTAT diversion pool is a stress-test ceiling, not free stock. [3, 8]

Decision

Verify contracts, packhouse throughput, and the economics of shifting fruit from existing customers.

04 / PRODUCT & ACCESS

“Avocado” is not one interchangeable SKU

USDA reports that most non-Hass U.S. imports come from the Dominican Republic. APHIS requirements also depend on origin and product; Guatemala’s Hass pathway has specific pest-control conditions. [8, 9]

Decision

Check cultivar, size, ripeness program, phytosanitary status, and current ACIR conditions before qualifying an origin.

METHOD & LIMITS

What these numbers can—and cannot—say.

Observed: FAOSTAT annual production and bilateral exports; USDA ERS monthly U.S. fresh-avocado imports. All physical quantities are normalized to metric tonnes. USDA values are customs import values, not shelf prices.

Short-horizon tabletop: February or July 2025 USDA ERS monthly import tonnes are converted to a weekly rate by dividing by days in the month and multiplying by seven. Lost Mexican flow is reduced by an assumed uplift on observed non-Mexican imports and a one-time buffer measured as days of normal Mexican flow. The selected month is repeated for the chosen weeks; alternatives and buffer are hypothetical, not available capacity or verified store inventory.

Annual tail test: The separate Mexico-zero scenario holds 2024 U.S. import requirements fixed and reallocates a chosen fraction of other suppliers’ reported exports to non-U.S. markets. It assumes no first-year production growth, substitution, inventory drawdown, or logistics expansion.

Important limit: FAOSTAT “Avocados” is not a variety-specific match to USDA’s fresh-avocado series. Export and import reporters differ in timing and coverage. Annual exports do not establish monthly availability, quality, route, contractual freedom, or U.S. approval. The premium control illustrates arithmetic; historical data here cannot identify a causal price response.
